name: Femi Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. Could you take me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Femi Baker, 58, a junior wheel-loader driver at a large mine after coming into the trade late with only secondary school. I check the bucket pins, load trucks and clear stone near the hopper, though I still ask my supervisor to check difficult loading angles. I like a clean pass into the pile and hate the sound when rock catches wrong. My wife Ada runs a pharmacy counter, our children are grown, and the mine pay has let us save more than six months' bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the loader still needs someone to feel when the bucket is biting too deep. I'd tell my brother the computer may save office time, but my shift looks much the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I'm junior, and that matters if the mine has to choose who gets the best shifts. The wage is good, but Ada's pharmacy pay wouldn't cover everything if my hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the loader shifts and ask my supervisor to check my loading angle at the north hopper. Set aside one pay packet for future house repairs instead of changing our weekly spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't feel a new threat in this picture. I feel the ordinary pressure of being a late learner on a machine that pays our biggest bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the north hopper difficult?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stone there is damp after rain and the pile slumps toward the truck lane. Last week I dug too low and had to back out slowly while my supervisor waved me clear. That lesson stays in my hands longer than a screen message would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you saving for with the next pay packet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The back wall of our house takes water when it rains hard. We can afford the repair, but I want a separate pot for it before it turns into a bigger bill. Our grown children pay their own rent now, so there's some room.

I'd tell my brother the computer may save **office time**, but my shift looks much the same.
think: I know I'm **junior**, and that matters if the mine has to choose who gets the best shifts.
The wage is good, but Ada's **pharmacy pay** wouldn't cover everything if my hours fell.
do: Keep the **loader shifts** and ask my supervisor to check my loading angle at the north hopper.
Set aside **one pay packet** for future house repairs instead of changing our weekly spending.
feel: **Mostly settled**, with the usual worry that I came into this trade late.
S0.quote: The wage is good, but Ada's pharmacy pay wouldn't cover everything if my hours fell.
fieldNote: He sees **seniority**, rather than mild AI, as the main limit on his security at the mine.
He has a **strong cushion** and good wages, yet he still checks his technique because his late entry weighs on him.

steps.text: Continue wheel-loader shifts and practise loading at the north hopper
Add one mine pay packet to the house repair fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch and buying might change first, while our loaders still need drivers on the rough ground. I'd ask the supervisor for clear instructions before any new screen gets fitted in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine stops replacing office staff, it may put more checking on drivers without more pay. I don't use AI tools, and I don't want to pretend I can learn a new screen overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a paper log of load counts and delays while any new dispatch system settles. Ask the supervisor for a demonstration of the cab screen before taking instructions from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the cab changing and the office shrinking. That unsettles me, although I still expect to be paid for driving the loader for the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into that log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads, long waits and any route that puts a truck too close to the hopper. I already write notes in a small book when a shift gets messy. If a screen starts deciding routes, I want a record I can understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the screen after a demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with my supervisor beside me for the first few loads. I'm slow with unfamiliar technology, but I can follow a clear sequence. I won't tap at it blindly while a truck is backing up.

I'd ask the supervisor for **clear instructions** before any new screen gets fitted in the cab.
think: If the mine stops replacing **office staff**, it may put more checking on drivers without more pay.
I don't use **AI tools**, and I don't want to pretend I can learn a new screen overnight.
do: Keep a **paper log** of load counts and delays while any new dispatch system settles.
Ask the **supervisor** for a demonstration of the cab screen before taking instructions from it.
feel: **Uneasy** about new instructions coming through a screen, though the loader still needs me.
S1.quote: I don't use AI tools, and I don't want to pretend I can learn a new screen overnight.
fieldNote: He expects **desk functions** to change before wheel-loader operation and asks for familiar, supervised instruction.
His **paper log** is a way to protect against mistakes, while his refusal to claim AI fluency fits his cautious manner.

steps.text: Keep a paper log of load counts during dispatch changes
Ask the supervisor for a cab-screen demonstration before using it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 AGI could run the plans and records, with robot loaders coming around 2031. I'd ask management to spell out which drivers would get training or other equipment work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 60 when the thinking work changes and about 63 when robots could run my loader. I haven't earned enough years in this job to assume retirement will carry Ada and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Request a written transfer policy from my supervisor this month and keep driving while I have shifts. Apply for a grader vacancy at another nearby mine if ours announces loader cuts after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get a tight feeling thinking about the loader standing empty. The savings stop me from panicking, but a lost mine wage at 63 would be a serious cut to our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a grader instead of another loader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've watched graders keep haul roads flat after heavy weather, and I know there are people driving them at neighbouring mines. I'd need instruction before I could do it safely. I would apply for a vacancy and tell them honestly what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ada say about applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada would ask how long the commute is and whether I'd lose the savings by buying another vehicle. One mine is only a longer bus ride; another would be too far. We'd do the sums before I accepted anything.

say: I'd tell the crew **2028 AGI** could run the plans and records, with robot loaders coming around 2031.
I'd ask management to spell out **which drivers** would get training or other equipment work.
think: I'd be **60** when the thinking work changes and about 63 when robots could run my loader.
I haven't earned enough years in this job to assume **retirement** will carry Ada and me.
do: Request a **written transfer policy** from my supervisor this month and keep driving while I have shifts.
Apply for a **grader vacancy** at another nearby mine if ours announces loader cuts after robots arrive.
feel: **Frightened** that the good wage could end while I'm still paying for ordinary life.
S2.quote: I haven't earned enough years in this job to assume retirement will carry Ada and me.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 desk changes** from the robot date that threatens his own driving income around 2031.
His savings give him choices, but he does not treat **age 63** as proof he can retire from paid work.

steps.text: Keep paid loader shifts while seeking the mine’s transfer policy
Apply for grader vacancies at a nearby mine if loader cuts begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the mine to show us its plan before AGI arrives in 2031. I'd remind my team that robot loaders follow around 2034, so driving isn't safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when AGI arrives, I'd still want the option to work; robots three years later might remove it. I'd rather learn another machine than sit in a classroom about software I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask to shadow the grader crew for two shifts this year if the supervisor agrees. Enrol in a paid grader course if the mine offers one before robot loaders reach our pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The years give me a chance to ask for training without dropping the loader wage. I'm still anxious because the grader could face the same machine problem later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't a grader be automated too by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could be, and I can't know which equipment goes first. The course would at least let me work there while jobs exist, and perhaps qualify me for a different site. I'm not calling it a lifelong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the course have to be paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss loader pay to attend. Ada and I have savings, but those are for our living costs and the house, not a mine's equipment plan. If the company needs workers to shift, it should give us paid time.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for the mine to show us its plan before AGI arrives in 2031.
I'd remind my team that **robot loaders** follow around 2034, so driving isn't safe forever.
think: At **63** when AGI arrives, I'd still want the option to work; robots three years later might remove it.
I'd rather learn another **machine** than sit in a classroom about software I don't trust.
do: Ask to **shadow the grader crew** for two shifts this year if the supervisor agrees.
Enrol in a **paid grader course** if the mine offers one before robot loaders reach our pit.
feel: **Concerned**, but less cornered because I could learn another machine while still earning.
S3.quote: I'd rather learn another machine than sit in a classroom about software I don't trust.
fieldNote: He uses the extra time for **grader exposure**, a concrete bridge from his current equipment work.
The proposed **course is conditional** on paid access; he will not risk household savings on an uncertain credential.

steps.text: Shadow the grader crew for two shifts if the supervisor agrees
Enrol in a paid grader course if the mine offers one
Keep earning loader wages while learning grader work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 AGI gives us a decade to see what actually happens to mine offices. I'd tell younger drivers the 2039 robot date is the one they need to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 for AGI and about 71 for robots, I might already have left the mine, but I can't bank on it. Our savings are real; the cost of later life is still a guess, especially if Ada stops work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Review our household figures with Ada every winter before deciding when I can leave paid work. Keep taking loader shifts while my health, the mine and our budget allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is time to make a measured decision. I still feel a little uneasy because money that looks ample today may have to last a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes on the winter list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House bills, Ada's wages, mine pay, what we have saved and what repairs may be waiting. Our children are grown, so school costs aren't in it. I want the figures on one page instead of a hopeful guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you leave the mine before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps. I don't enjoy night shifts as much as I did when I started, but I like having work that matters and pays. I'd decide from our health and the accounts, not from a date on a card.

say: I'd say **2036 AGI** gives us a decade to see what actually happens to mine offices.
I'd tell younger drivers the **2039 robot date** is the one they need to plan around.
think: At **68** for AGI and about 71 for robots, I might already have left the mine, but I can't bank on it.
Our savings are real; the cost of **later life** is still a guess, especially if Ada stops work too.
do: Review our **household figures** with Ada every winter before deciding when I can leave paid work.
Keep taking **loader shifts** while my health, the mine and our budget allow.
feel: **More patient** than in the fast case, with a nagging doubt about the cost of stopping work.
S4.quote: Our savings are real; the cost of later life is still a guess, especially if Ada stops work too.
fieldNote: A ten-year runway allows an annual **budget check** with his wife rather than an immediate job switch.
He expects to be **71** when hands-on robots arrive and remains cautious about assuming either health or retirement income.

steps.text: Review retirement income and household bills with Ada each winter
Continue paid loader shifts while health and budget allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, worries me most. It could bring robot loaders by about 2031, when I'd be 63 and maybe still needing that wage. A clear transfer rule and a paid chance to learn another machine would help. The loader pays well enough to make me cautious and late enough to make me replaceable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how many of the drivers are learning their first mine machine late in life. I know two others who came from warehouse work. They look confident from the office window, but both ask for help when the pile is unstable. Any training plan has to reach us, not just the people who already know every machine.

headlineQuote: The loader pays well enough to make me cautious and late enough to make me replaceable.
portrait: Femi is a **58-year-old** junior wheel-loader operator who came to mining late and still asks for help with difficult loads.
His **mine pay** is high for the job, and his savings cover more than six months of household expenses.
His wife works at a **pharmacy counter**, and their grown children no longer depend on school-age spending.
He avoids **AI tools** and wants to hold on to paid equipment work while weighing each possible change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because robot loaders around 2031 could end the mine wage before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear transfer rule** and a paid chance to learn another machine would help him act without gambling the household savings.
